question.text:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

  1. The probability that a fair coin lands on tails $45$ times out of $80$ coin flips.
  2. The probability of getting $4$ even numbers on $6$ rolls of a $6$-sided die.
  3. The probability that a fair spinner with four regions, red, green, yellow, and blue, lands on green at least $27$ times out of $60$ spins.
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have $n=80$ and $p=\dfrac12.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 80\cdot 0.5\\[5pt] &= 40 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 80\cdot (1-0.5) \\[5pt] &=40 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation II, we have $n=6$ and $p=\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &=6\cdot 0.5\\[5pt] &=3\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation III, we have $n=60$ and $p=\dfrac14.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 60 \cdot 0.25\\[5pt] &= 15 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 60\cdot \left(1-0.25\right) \\[5pt] &=45 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

  3. The probability that an archer hits the bull's eye more than $10$ times out of $25$ attempts if the probability of hitting the bull's eye on a single shot is $0.56.$

question.text:
Given that the random variable $X\sim B(90,0.47),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(40\leq X < 50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.07 \,$$\, 0.08 \,$$\, 0.09 \,$
$\, -0.6 \,$ $\, 0.2514 \,$ $\, 0.2483 \,$ $\, 0.2451 \,$
$\, -0.5 \,$ $\, 0.2843 \,$ $\, 0.2810 \,$ $\, 0.2776 \,$
$\, -0.4 \,$ $\, 0.3192 \,$ $\, 0.3156 \,$ $\, 0.3121 \,$
$z$$\, 0.00 \,$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$
$\, 1.4 \,$ $\, 0.9192 \,$ $\, 0.9207 \,$ $\, 0.9222 \,$
$\, 1.5 \,$ $\, 0.9332 \,$ $\, 0.9345 \,$ $\, 0.9357 \,$
$\, 1.6 \,$ $\, 0.9452 \,$ $\, 0.9463 \,$ $\, 0.9474 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=90$ and $p = 0.47.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 90\cdot 0.47\\[5pt] &= 42.3 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 90\cdot (1-0.47) \\[5pt] &=47.7 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (90)(0.47) = 42.3 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (90)(0.47)(1-0.47) = 22.419. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(42.3, 22.419).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(40 \leq X < 50).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(40 \leq X < 50) = P(40 \leq X \leq 49) \approx P(39.5 \leq Y \leq 49.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(39.5 \leq Y \leq 49.5) &= P\left(\dfrac{39.5-42.3}{\sqrt{22.419}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{49.5-42.3}{\sqrt{22.419}}\right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( -0.59 \leq Z \leq 1.52 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z\leq 1.52) - P(Z < -0.59) \\[5pt] &= P(Z\leq 1.52) - P(Z \leq -0.59) \\[5pt] &=\Phi(1.52)-\Phi(-0.59) \\[5pt] &=0.9357-0.2776 \\[5pt] &=0.6581 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(40 \leq X < 50) \approx 0.658. \] Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.6587.$

example.title: Using a Normal Approximation to Approximate a Binomial Probability Over an Interval

question.text:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

  1. The probability that a fair coin lands on tails $5$ times out of $8$ coin flips.
  2. The probability of choosing $5$ men in a neighborhood with $40$ adults if the probability that a randomly selected adult is a man is $0.55.$
  3. The probability that a golf player makes less than $3$ putts in $15$ shots at the same hole if the probability of making a putt in each shot is $0.3.$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have $n=8$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 8\cdot 0.5\\[5pt] &= 4\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation II, we have $n=40$ and $p=0.55.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 40\cdot 0.55\\[5pt] &= 22 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 40\cdot (1-0.55) \\[5pt] &=18 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation III, we have $n=15$ and $p=0.3.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 15\cdot 0.3\\[5pt] &=4.5\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

  2. The probability of getting $7$ ones on $10$ rolls of a $4$-sided die.
  3. The probability of getting $32$ odd numbers on $80$ rolls of a $6$-sided die.

  • In situation II, we have $n=10$ and $p=\dfrac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 10\cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{2}\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.
